description: We are engineering students taking part in the NASA Space Apps Challenge to gain experience, learn new skills, and work on something interesting. We have a strong interest in space exploration, especially spacecraft. We're looking forward to working with others, sharing ideas, and gaining practical experience through this challenge. We welcome anyone interested in space, engineering, programming, or design.
summary: We built Footprints on Mars and the Moon, an interactive website that helps school-age space enthusiasts discover the machines left behind after their missions ended. Visitors can spin 3D globes, follow a timeline to find landing sites, and explore spacecraft through models, mission photographs, and imagined stories told in the spacecraft’s own voices. On the Moon, learners see how Surveyor helped pave the way for Apollo and where the Apollo landing stages stayed behind. On Mars, they learn how Phoenix used its robotic arm to uncover water ice and how InSight listened for marsquakes to study the planet’s interior. By showing how each machine worked and what it taught us, our project makes space history easier to explore and shows why these missions still matter long after their final signals.
details:
Our team(Silent Rovers) developed "Footprints on the moon and mars", an interactive website that tells the stories of spacecraft left behind after their missions ended. Visitors choose Mars or the Moon, rotate a 3D globe or use a timeline to see when and where different missions landed. They can explore spacecraft models, mission photographs, and short stories that explain what each machine was built to do, what it discovered, and what happened when its mission ended.

Our creative approach was to let the spacecraft tell parts of their own stories. The voices are imagined, but the stories are based on real mission facts. On Mars, visitors can learn how Phoenix used its robotic arm to uncover water ice. On the Moon, they can see how the Surveyor landers helped prepare for Apollo and where the Apollo landing stages stayed behind. These examples connect the design of each machine to theexploration it made possible.

We built the website using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a custom WordPress theme. We used Three.js for the interactive 3D views and pixabay for sound effects. We used NASA mission pages, photographs, and published 3D models as references and credited the source material on the site. We used Claude and ChatGPT to assist with coding, draft stories, and prepare 3D assets for the web. Our team reviewed the content and tested the experience, and we used text-to-speech for the spacecraft voices.

We designed the site for school-age learners and casual space enthusiasts. We considered how to keep the language clear, distinguish imagined dialogue from historical facts. Even when a browser cannot display 3D graphics. Those visitors can still read the mission information in a list. We want young learners to come away with a simple idea: a spacecraft can stop sending signals, but what it taught us can shape the next mission.
